narrative: A 25-year-old Syrian mother and her family left Syria in November, worn down by a war that after seven years seemed to have no end. They tried to settle in Izmir, Turkey, but after only a month there they felt trapped, so they borrowed money to pay smugglers to help them cross the Aegean, arriving on the Greek island of Lesbos in December. Under the EU-Turkey deal, Lesbos had become a processing center and they were not allowed to leave the island until their asylum request was decided - a process that, with an understaffed asylum service, could take months, with lengthy appeals if rejected. The Moria camp was so overcrowded that after a couple of days the family left and improvised a tent on a nearby hill dotted with olive trees, built from salvaged wood, rusting metal rods and recycled tarp that leaked in the rain. Trash lined the corridors of the camp and the toilets overflowed; women shared tents with unrelated men, and other women warned her not to walk around alone because of drug dealers and drunks. The hardest thing, she said, was trying to find a proper place to get clean.
